raw_response:
Well, I've been farming these 12 mu for 35 years now. I'm 49, my wife and I do most of the work — our child is in school and can't help much. We're a small family, only three of us, so every yuan matters. We can't afford to waste money on fancy inputs like some of the bigger farms.

My wheat is already in the ground from last October — 8 mu of it. It's looking okay so far, not great but not bad. I saved most of the seed myself, bought a little fresh seed to mix in. Costs less that way, about 25 yuan per mu for the new seed. I'll topdress with urea soon, maybe around Qingming, when the wheat starts greening up. I bought two big bags of urea and one bag of compound fertilizer for the wheat. I put the compound fertilizer down before planting last autumn, so now it's just the topdress. I also need to irrigate three times for the wheat — once now if it stays dry, once at jointing, and once at filling. The pump electricity adds up, so if it rains I skip one. I expect about 420 kg per mu, maybe a bit more if the weather cooperates. Last year was a bit dry so I'm hoping for better.

Come early June, the wheat comes off and I need to get maize in the ground fast — sometimes only five or six days between harvest and planting. I hire the tractor guy to plow quick, costs money but you can't plant maize by hand on 8 mu in time. I use hybrid seed for maize, that's 45 yuan per mu, expensive but worth it. For fertilizer, I do one base application of compound fertilizer at planting, then topdress with urea when the maize is knee-high. Same amounts as wheat roughly — about 14 kg of nitrogen per mu total, but I don't think in kilograms, I think in bags. One bag of compound for every three mu, one bag of urea for every two mu. I irrigate maize twice, maybe three times if it's a dry summer. I expect about 480 kg per mu.

My wife manages the vegetable plots. We have 1.5 mu of cabbage, half a mu of cauliflower, half a mu of chili, and half a mu of eggplant. The cabbage and cauliflower go in mid-March — we already started the seedlings in the courtyard. They need a lot of manure and fertilizer. I bought some chicken manure from the poultry farm down the road, plus extra urea. Cabbage especially is hungry — I put down base fertilizer and then topdress twice more. The chili and eggplant get transplanted in early May. Vegetables need more spraying too — herbicide and insecticide. I can't afford the expensive stuff, so I use what the supply shop recommends for cheap. Vegetables bring good cash at the Quzhou market, but they're risky. If the price drops, you lose money. That's why I only keep 3 mu total in vegetables — can't risk everything.

I still have that 1 mu of stevia on the north side. Planted it two years ago. It's a funny crop — doesn't need much, just some compound fertilizer and about three irrigations. No pesticides really, bugs don't bother it much. The buyer comes to the village to collect it in early October. Yield is maybe 250 kg per mu of dried leaves. It's not huge money but it's steady.

For labor, it's mostly my wife and me. I hire a couple of day-laborers for wheat harvest and maize harvest — the window is tight and two people can't cut and thresh 8 mu fast enough. I pay them about 100 yuan per day, plus meals. For the vegetables, my wife does the transplanting and picking, I help with watering and hauling. Sometimes we hire one person for cabbage harvest if it's a big load.

This year fertilizer prices are still high, so I'm being careful. I thought about putting more on the maize, but I need to keep some cash for the vegetables and for my daughter's school expenses. I'd rather apply a bit too much on the wheat than too little — a bad wheat year hurts more than wasting a little fertilizer. Total I'm spending about 4,600 yuan on inputs this year, including seeds, fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation electricity, and hired labor. That's a big chunk of our savings. I hope the grain prices don't drop.
